issues.label: Standard of review for subjective fear of persecution
Connection of fear to one of the five Convention grounds
Failure to consider evidence of seeking protection from authorities
Analysis of fear under paragraph 97(1)(b) of the Act
Certification of serious question of general importance
Remedy: dismissal of application for judicial review

result.overall: The Court dismissed the application for judicial review, finding no patently unreasonable error in the panel's conclusion that the applicant did not have a subjective fear of persecution and that the panel properly analyzed the applicant's fear under paragraph 97(1)(b) of the Act.

themes.name: Subjective fear of persecution
themes.summary: Whether the applicant demonstrated a genuine subjective fear of persecution as required for refugee status.

themes.name: Connection to Convention grounds
themes.summary: Whether the applicant's fear of persecution was connected to one of the five Convention grounds.

themes.name: Government protection
themes.summary: Whether the applicant rebutted the presumption that the government could protect him.

themes.name: Analysis under paragraph 97(1)(b) of the Act
themes.summary: Whether the panel properly analyzed the applicant's fear of death threats under paragraph 97(1)(b) of the Act.

arguments.quote: The questions submitted by the applicant are the following: 1. Is the applicant's conduct consistent with a subjective fear of persecution?
arguments.claim: The applicant argues that his conduct is consistent with a subjective fear of persecution.

arguments.quote: The personal vengeance of Villareal, who was connected to the government, had a direct link to the Convention because of his alleged political opinions.
arguments.claim: The applicant claims that the personal vengeance is connected to a Convention ground due to political opinions.

arguments.quote: The panel made an error when it concluded that the applicant did not seek protection from the authorities in his country.
arguments.claim: The applicant argues the panel erred in concluding he did not seek protection from authorities.

arguments.quote: The panel did not analyze the applicant's fear of death threats under paragraph 97(1)(b) of the Act.
arguments.claim: The applicant claims the panel failed to analyze his fear under paragraph 97(1)(b) of the Act.

arguments.quote: In order to meet the definition of a "Convention refugee", the applicant must show that he meets all parts of that definition.
arguments.claim: The respondent argues the applicant must meet all parts of the refugee definition, including subjective and objective fear, connection to Convention grounds, and lack of government protection.

arguments.quote: The panel was entirely free to assess whether a subjective fear of persecution existed in view of the claimant for asylum's actions after the events on which he based his claim.
arguments.claim: The respondent submits that the panel's assessment of subjective fear is a factual and credibility determination not warranting court intervention unless patently unreasonable.
arguments.authority: Canada (Minister of Employment and Immigration) v. Dan-Ash

arguments.quote: The existence of a connection between the alleged persecution and one of the five Convention grounds is a question of fact, which is therefore within the purview of the panel's expertise.
arguments.claim: The respondent argues that the connection to Convention grounds is a factual matter within the panel's expertise.
arguments.authority: Leon v. Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration)

arguments.quote: The panel was right to conclude that the applicant did not establish a lack of government protection in Mexico.
arguments.claim: The respondent contends the panel correctly found the applicant did not rebut the presumption of government protection.
arguments.authority: Ward; Kadenko v. Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration)

arguments.quote: The panel assessed the various pieces of evidence about actions taken by the applicant to obtain protection from the authorities against the persecuting agent Villareal.
arguments.claim: The respondent states the panel considered evidence of the applicant's attempts to seek protection and found explanations unsatisfactory.

arguments.quote: In its reasons, the panel addressed the asylum application made pursuant to paragraph 97(1)(b) of the Act.
arguments.claim: The respondent argues the panel properly addressed the applicant's claim under paragraph 97(1)(b) of the Act.

holdings.quote: I answer the first and fourth questions in the negative, I do not need to answer the other two questions and the application for judicial review will be dismissed.
holdings.statement: The Court dismisses the application, answering negatively the questions on subjective fear and analysis under paragraph 97(1)(b), and declines to answer other questions.

holdings.quote: The Court should not intervene in such a case unless the panel has made a patently unreasonable error.
holdings.statement: The standard of review for subjective fear of persecution is deferential; intervention only if patently unreasonable error.

holdings.quote: This conclusion seems entirely reasonable to the Court and therefore cannot be the subject of any intervention by the Court.
holdings.statement: The panel's conclusion that the applicant lacked subjective fear is reasonable based on his conduct and thus not subject to intervention.

holdings.quote: In addition to the points listed by the panel, there are other facts which show that the applicant did not really have a subjective fear of persecution.
holdings.statement: Additional facts such as failure to seek protection in the U.S. and return to Mexico support the finding of no subjective fear.

holdings.quote: As the applicant has not been able to establish a subjective fear of persecution, an essential component of the refugee definition, there is no need to proceed with the analysis of the other parts of that definition.
holdings.statement: Failure to establish subjective fear means no need to analyze connection to Convention grounds or government protection.

holdings.quote: The analysis of the applicant's actions by the panel on page 3 of its decision persuades the Court that this question was dealt with and the conclusion was not unreasonable.
holdings.statement: The panel did analyze the applicant's fear under paragraph 97(1)(b) and its conclusion was reasonable.

holdings.quote: In the absence of any patently unreasonable error in this decision, I have no intention of intervening.
holdings.statement: The Court will not intervene as there is no patently unreasonable error in the panel's decision.

holdings.quote: The parties declined the offer to submit a serious question of general importance.
holdings.statement: No serious question of general importance is certified as parties declined to submit one.

holdings.quote: The application for judicial review is dismissed.
holdings.statement: The Court dismisses the application for judicial review.

rebuttals.quote: The personal vengeance of Villareal, who was connected to the government, had a direct link to the Convention because of his alleged political opinions.
rebuttals.point: The personal vengeance is connected to a Convention ground due to political opinions.
rebuttals.court_answer: The Court rejects this as the panel found the vengeance was personal and not connected to Convention grounds.

authorities.quote: Among these parts are the subjective and objective components of the alleged fear of persecution, the existence of a connection between that alleged fear and one of the Convention grounds and the absence of government protection (Canada (Attorney General) v. Ward, [1993] 2 S.C.R. 689, at 723-726).
authorities.why: The Court follows Ward for the elements of the refugee definition including subjective and objective fear, connection to Convention grounds, and government protection.

authorities.quote: As the question is one of assessment of facts and credibility, intervention by the Court is not warranted unless the panel has made a patently unreasonable error (Canada (Minister of Employment and Immigration) v. Dan-Ash (1988), 93 N.R. 33 (F.C.A.)).
authorities.authority: Canada (Minister of Employment and Immigration) v. Dan-Ash
authorities.why: The Court follows Dan-Ash for the standard of review on factual and credibility assessments.

authorities.quote: The existence of a connection between the alleged persecution and one of the five Convention grounds is a question of fact, which is therefore within the purview of the panel's expertise (Leon v. Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration, _1995_ F.C.J. No. 1253 (F.C.T.D.) (QL)).
authorities.authority: Leon v. Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration)
authorities.why: The Court follows Leon for the panel's expertise on connection to Convention grounds.

authorities.quote: Unless the governmental system has collapsed completely, a government is presumed able to protect its citizens (Ward, supra; Kadenko v. Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration) (1996), 206 N.R. 272 (F.C.A.), _1996_F.C.J. No. 1376 (F.C.A.) (QL)).
authorities.authority: Ward; Kadenko v. Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration)
authorities.why: The Court follows Ward and Kadenko for the presumption of government protection unless the system has collapsed.

left_open.quote: Does the alleged fear of persecution, namely personal vengeance, have any connection with one of the five Convention grounds?
left_open.issue: Connection of fear to one of the five Convention grounds
left_open.reason: No need to decide because applicant failed to establish subjective fear of persecution.

left_open.quote: Did the panel fail to consider evidence showing that the applicant actually sought protection from the authorities in his country?
left_open.issue: Failure to consider evidence of seeking protection from authorities
left_open.reason: No need to decide because applicant failed to establish subjective fear of persecution.
